narrative.summary: When Beatrice Dunmore, the respected supervisor of the Blackthorn archaeological dig, is found stabbed with an antique letter opener, suspicion falls heavily on Ambrose Rutherford, the local landowner, due to his known conflicts with her. The dig's official archival records, endorsed by the village elder Ivor Ormesby, appear to confirm a timeline placing the murder within Ambrose’s alibi gap. However, Frances Orme, the village schoolteacher and amateur detective, suspects the archival records were manipulated to protect the real culprit. Through rigorous examination, Frances uncovers a forged excavation report, crafted to mislead by exploiting the authority of the village elder and archivist. The mystery hinges on revealing who truly controlled the archival narrative and how the official record was manipulated to misplace the time and evidence of the murder.

accepted_facts: Beatrice Dunmore was stabbed with an antique letter opener to the heart.
The letter opener was kept in the village archive room by Ottoline Thorne.
Ambrose Rutherford and Ottoline Thorne had motives relating to the dig's outcome.
The official excavation report was dated weeks before the murder and widely accepted.
Village elder Ivor Ormesby endorsed the archival documents as authentic.
Ottoline Thorne had access to the archival documents and means to forge them.
The victim died between quarter past nine and quarter past ten.
inferred_conclusions: The archival report was chemically treated to simulate ink aging, deceiving basic forensic tests.
The paper watermark date contradicts the stated report date, proving forgery.
Ottoline Thorne had the unique capability and opportunity to forge the report.
The murder was timed to exploit trust in archival authority, creating a false timeline alibi for Ambrose Rutherford.
The letter opener’s handling marks misdirect suspicion to Josephine Whitlock but actual disturbances connect to Ottoline Thorne.

mechanism.description: Ottoline Thorne forged an excavation report dated weeks before the murder by chemically aging the ink to simulate natural oxidation. The forged report was endorsed by village elder Ivor Ormesby, whose authority caused the village to accept it unquestioningly. The paper's watermark date and archival stamps, which Ottoline overlooked or misrepresented, contradict the report's stated date, exposing the forgery. This forgery created a false timeline placing Beatrice Dunmore's discovery earlier, allowing Ottoline to murder her without suspicion by exploiting the authority of archival endorsements and social trust.

delivery_path.step: Ottoline chemically treated the ink to simulate aging on forged report.

Official archival records accepted and used to establish timeline.
Ottoline stabbed Beatrice during the real timeline gap, relying on false archival date.

outcome.result: The forgery and endorsement misled the village into accepting a false timeline, allowing the culprit to evade suspicion until Frances Orme exposed the deception through forensic document analysis and social logic.

false_assumption.statement: The archival documents endorsed by village elder Ivor Ormesby are authentic and reliable evidence of the timeline.
false_assumption.why_it_seems_reasonable: Ivor Ormesby's longstanding respected position and trusted role in village affairs led everyone to accept archival records without question.
false_assumption.what_it_hides: The archival report has been forged by chemical ink aging and archival filing tampering, creating a false timeline that protects the real culprit.

false_solution.the_one_flaw: The forged archival report's paper watermark date contradicts the report's claimed date, impossible for Ambrose to have manipulated.

The discriminating chemical test (early act 3) uses only previously exposed evidence to confirm forgery and link Ottoline to the murder.
